evaluation.positioning_hook: A status-conscious Texas matriarch discovers her son’s exorcist is a centuries-old parasite using demonology to hijack her family, and must outmaneuver him before he rewires everyone she loves.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The script has a clean, sellable engine: wealthy family, occult possession, and a mother fighting to save her son and status. The hook is easy to pitch and the escalating set-pieces give it real trailer value, though the tonal bite will skew it more to genre buyers than four-quadrant audiences.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The premise lands immediately in the opening pages with D.J.’s strange energy event, Carol’s social world, and Andrew’s arrival as the family fixer. By the time the demonologist reveal hits, the script has already established a clear, ownable engine.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Carol is a strong lead: funny, status-aware, maternal, and increasingly ferocious as the story turns. Andrew is a memorable antagonist with charisma and menace, and D.J. gives the story a volatile emotional center, though the supporting cast is more functional than deeply layered.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The script’s blend of upper-class domestic satire, occult possession, and racial/class power politics is unusually specific. The choice to make the demonology a tool of social control rather than pure supernatural horror gives the material a sharper, more contemporary edge.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The story keeps escalating through the party, the injury, the exorcism, the legal pressure, the road capture, and the final showdown. Each turn adds a new layer of threat or reversal, and the script is especially strong when Carol’s certainty collapses into action.

resonant_originality.reasoning: The central idea feels fresh because it fuses a recognizable possession framework with wealth, assimilation, and family complicity. The demon as a mechanism of privilege and control is immediately legible and gives the genre premise a social sting.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: The Paxton house, the catered parties, the golf-club money, the legal machinery, and the family hierarchy all create a vivid social ecosystem. The world feels story-generating because every room contains a power dynamic, not just a plot function.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The script has a distinct register: glossy, biting, and increasingly unhinged without losing the domestic comedy of manners underneath. Carol’s one-liners, the family’s coded cruelty, and the occult escalation create a tone that is hard to mistake for generic horror.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: There are deeper currents around assimilation, maternal sacrifice, class performance, and inherited shame, and the script keeps revealing them through behavior rather than speeches. It is still primarily a surface-forward genre piece, but the social subtext gives it more aftertaste than a standard possession thriller.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: Carol, Matt, D.J., Beverly, Roy, and Andrew all generate friction in different combinations, and the family table scenes are as playable as the horror beats. The script has a strong relational engine because every alliance is conditional and every conversation can flip power.

lead_characters.name: Carol Paxton
lead_characters.demographics: Woman, late 30s to early 40s, Latina-presenting but not strictly defined, affluent suburban mother, married, Texas-based.
lead_characters.hook: Carol is the polished queen bee of a wealthy Texas household who has spent years converting survival instincts into social grace. She loves her son fiercely, knows exactly how to work a room, and slowly realizes the family’s comfort is built on a moral rot she has been helping maintain.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Toni Collette in Hereditary or Julia Louis-Dreyfus in Veep when the mask starts cracking — a role that lets an actor play wit, vanity, maternal devotion, panic, and righteous fury in the same frame.

lead_characters.name: Andrew Collinsworth
lead_characters.demographics: Man, 70s, English, older, imposing, charismatic, occult practitioner.
lead_characters.hook: Andrew presents as the family’s elegant, worldly fixer, but he is really the story’s predator in a bespoke suit: ancient, amused, and always several moves ahead. He weaponizes charm, class fluency, and spiritual authority to turn the household into his instrument.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of villain role that gives an actor the delicious control of Ralph Fiennes in The Menu or Christoph Waltz in Inglourious Basterds — refined menace, verbal precision, and the chance to pivot from courtly to monstrous on a dime.

lead_characters.name: David
lead_characters.demographics: Male, mid-teens, affluent teen, musically gifted, emotionally volatile.
lead_characters.hook: D.J. is the son Carol has tried to raise outside the family’s old poison, which makes him both the emotional prize and the easiest target. He is sweet, artistic, and vulnerable, but the script keeps testing how much of him is selfhood and how much is inherited corruption.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is strong young-actor material in the lane of Lucas Hedges in Manchester by the Sea or Justice Smith in The Get Down — a role that asks for sensitivity, confusion, charm, and a late-story turn into something unsettling.

lead_characters.name: Beverly Paxton
lead_characters.demographics: Woman, late 70s, wealthy matriarch, white, Southern social power broker.
lead_characters.hook: Beverly is the family’s velvet-gloved enforcer, the kind of matriarch who can insult you while making it sound like hospitality. She is funny, poisonous, and deeply invested in keeping the family’s hierarchy intact.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is prime grande-dame territory in the vein of Jane Fonda in Grace and Frankie or Jessica Lange in Feud — a role that lets an actor play social authority, comic cruelty, and buried menace.

lead_characters.name: Matt Paxton
lead_characters.demographics: Man, 50s, wealthy businessman, white, husband and father, Texas elite.
lead_characters.hook: Matt is the family’s polished patriarch, a man who wants to believe he is the rational center of the house even as he keeps choosing convenience over truth. He is charming, evasive, and increasingly compromised by the system he benefits from.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a solid prestige-supporting role in the lane of Michael Shannon in a domestic thriller or Kyle Chandler in Bloodline — a chance to play authority, denial, and emotional collapse without ever becoming a cartoon.

lead_characters.name: Hayden
lead_characters.demographics: Female, mid-teens, Latina, working-class background, smart, principled.
lead_characters.hook: Hayden is the outsider who sees the Paxtons clearly because she has less to lose from their mythology. She is emotionally honest and morally steadier than the family around her, which makes her both a conscience and a target.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This gives a young actor the kind of grounded, emotionally legible material that made Auliʻi Cravalho in The Power or Xochitl Gomez in The Baby-Sitters Club pop — sincerity under pressure, with a real moral point of view.

lead_characters.name: Christina
lead_characters.demographics: Woman, 40s, Latina, mother, stressed, working-class or middle-class.
lead_characters.hook: Christina arrives as the practical parent trying to keep a crisis from becoming a catastrophe, and she quickly becomes the human counterweight to the Paxtons’ wealth and manipulation. She is wary, exhausted, and more perceptive than the room initially gives her credit for.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of grounded supporting role that lets an actor do lived-in realism in the mode of Patricia Clarkson in Pieces of April or America Ferrera in Real Women Have Curves — warmth, fatigue, and quiet authority.

lead_characters.name: Roy Paxton
lead_characters.demographics: Man, 80s, wealthy elder patriarch, white, politically connected.
lead_characters.hook: Roy is the old-money patriarch who treats power as inheritance and morality as a public-relations problem. He is blunt, entitled, and useful as a reminder that the family’s rot predates the current crisis.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a sharp elder-statesman role in the lane of J.K. Simmons in Whiplash or Brian Cox in Succession — a chance to play institutional power, contempt, and comic menace.

lead_characters.name: Emilia Rodriguez
lead_characters.hook: Emilia is the legal adult in the room when the family tries to turn catastrophe into paperwork. She is professional, skeptical, and a useful pressure valve in the final stretch.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a clean, efficient character-actor role that gives an actor the authority and precision of a courtroom or negotiation scene without needing a giant arc.

lead_characters.name: Agent Lopez
lead_characters.hook: Lopez is the outside force who briefly punctures the family’s insulated reality and gives Carol a possible exit. She is calm, competent, and crucial to the final reveal that the system is larger than the house.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of crisp law-enforcement role that lets an actor play competence and moral clarity in the style of Regina King in a procedural or Carrie Coon in a thriller.

lead_characters.name: Agent O’Reilly
lead_characters.hook: O’Reilly is the second half of the federal intrusion, a functional but important presence in the climax. He exists to show how little ordinary authority matters once Andrew fully reveals himself.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a compact, scene-specific role for a strong character actor who can sell procedural authority before the supernatural escalation wipes it out.

older supporting roles require strong character-actor presence
Andrew needs an actor who can play charm and menace with a refined English accent

locations.interior_exterior_ratio: mostly interior with recurring exterior driveway/road/ramp scenes
notable_requirements: large affluent Texas house with pool-party scale
cramped working-class kitchen for Hayden's home

technical.vfx_details: telekinetic energy waves, body distortions, room-shaking effects, practical/digital possession moments, and a few supernatural death beats
technical.sfx_needs: blood, broken glass injury, dog attack, neck-break deaths, practical possession effects, syringe injection beats

platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Feature release model: streamer original, specialty theatrical, or premium genre label with adult content and elevated-horror positioning

budget.note: Contemporary interiors keep the footprint contained, but the possession effects, multiple night exteriors, dog attack, FBI arrival, and several supernatural death beats will need disciplined execution.

casting.note: Carol and Andrew are the load-bearing roles: Carol needs comic authority plus emotional collapse, and Andrew needs a very specific blend of elegance, age, and predatory charisma.

development.note: The script’s tonal balance between satire, family drama, and outright horror is distinctive, but buyers will track how cleanly the social commentary stays legible once the possession mechanics take over.

comp_set.title: Hereditary
comp_set.why_it_comps: Shares the escalating domestic-horror structure and the showcase role for a mother whose family crisis turns into a nightmare of inheritance and control.

comp_set.title: Get Out
comp_set.why_it_comps: The social-power critique is embedded inside a genre engine, with race, class, and family performance driving the horror rather than sitting beside it.

comp_set.title: Ready or Not
comp_set.why_it_comps: Matches the wealthy-family pressure cooker, the dark comic tone, and the heroine forced to fight a corrupt domestic system from inside the house.

comp_set.title: The Menu
comp_set.why_it_comps: Like this script, it weaponizes elite manners, status performance, and satirical cruelty before detonating into genre violence.

audience_target.primary_audience: Adult genre fans who like elevated horror with social bite, plus viewers drawn to sharp family satire and a strong female lead.
audience_target.demographics: 18-49 skew, slightly female-leaning, urban/suburban, streamer-friendly, horror-literate audience with appetite for prestige-genre hybrids.

budget_tier.note: A contemporary house-bound genre piece with moderate VFX, practical effects, and a limited cast should live in indie feature economics if the possession effects are kept disciplined.

lane_fit.detail: This sits naturally in the lane where social commentary, family dysfunction, and genre escalation are all part of the sell. The script has enough style and role meat to attract a filmmaker looking for a breakout horror feature with awards-adjacent texture.

ip_potential.detail: Standalone feature with a closed supernatural conflict and no clear sequel or spinoff vector beyond the core family story.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Carol is a real star role.
strengths.what_it_means: This gives the project a casting-forward center of gravity: a female lead who can carry comedy, social satire, and horror escalation without losing audience sympathy. That is exactly the kind of part that attracts actor-driven buyers and can elevate a genre package quickly.
strengths.evidence: Carol’s party-hosting poise, her private panic over D.J., her confrontation with Beverly, and her final pivot into violent agency all belong to one coherent character arc.

strengths.what_it_means: The script has a clean commercial sentence that buyers can understand in one pass, which lowers development friction and helps marketing immediately. That clarity is attractive to streamer film teams and genre labels looking for a high-concept hook with a prestige wrapper.
strengths.evidence: The demonologist reveal, the family exorcism, and the idea that the occult force is tied to wealth and control all land early and clearly.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The social satire is baked into the horror.
strengths.what_it_means: The script is not just a possession story; it is a class-and-race power story that uses genre to make the commentary feel entertaining rather than academic. That makes it more marketable to buyers who want elevated horror with a point of view.
strengths.evidence: Beverly’s “Latina angels” line, Andrew’s manipulation of the family’s money and status, and the repeated use of assimilation language all sharpen the genre engine.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The house is a story engine.
strengths.what_it_means: The Paxton mansion is not just a setting; it is a pressure chamber where every room reflects a different kind of power. That kind of contained, textured world is attractive because it keeps production focused while still feeling expansive on screen.
strengths.evidence: The kitchen, office, master bedroom, driveway, guest room, and ramp all function as distinct arenas for conflict.

strengths.what_it_means: A villain with charm, class fluency, and supernatural authority is a strong commercial asset because he can carry trailers, posters, and word-of-mouth. Buyers like antagonists who are as watchable as the protagonist, and Andrew absolutely is.
strengths.evidence: His refined accent, his “faith in me” pitch, his controlled exorcism, and his final escalation into open violence all make him legible and distinctive.

whats_special.headline: This is a clean elevated-horror package: a star-making lead role, a high-concept premise, and a contained luxury-house setting that keeps the economics sane. The social satire gives it a sharper buyer lane than standard possession fare, making it attractive to streamer film teams and prestige genre financiers looking for something with both bite and market shape.

items.area: The third-act possession rules keep shifting.
items.detail: Andrew moves from exorcist to manipulator to full telekinetic killer, and the script keeps widening what his power can do. That escalation is exciting, but buyers will notice that the mechanics are more elastic than fixed, which makes the final act feel tier-dependent on execution.

items.area: The satire sometimes competes with the horror.
items.detail: The script is strongest when class, race, and family control are embedded in the possession story, but a few stretches lean hard into speechifying or explanatory dialogue. That can be a feature for some buyers and a friction point for others if they want the genre engine to stay dominant.

items.area: Andrew is so dominant he narrows the ensemble.
items.detail: Once he fully takes over, the family’s other dynamics become reactive, and the story increasingly depends on Carol versus Andrew. That is a strong spine, but it reduces the amount of playable ensemble energy in the back half.

items.area: The ending lands on a hard tonal swing.
items.detail: The final beat of Carol settling into the household’s new order is a sharp satirical button, but it also asks the audience to accept a very dark moral inversion after a long horror escalation. Some buyers will love that bite; others will flag it as a tonal risk for broader genre audiences.

issues.headline: The main friction is tonal and mechanical: the script’s social satire is a strength, but it also makes the possession rules feel more fluid than fixed as the story escalates. Buyers will also clock that the back half becomes a very concentrated Carol-versus-Andrew showdown, which is effective but narrows the ensemble payoff.
